Read Manning & Massumi, Thought in the Act (selections — see Reading Guide) Bring one object to the (Im)material Potluck: something from your practice that is both material and immaterial, or that troubles that distinction Be prepared to describe: what it does, what it thinks, what it can't say "Making would already be thinking-in-action, and conceptualization a practice in its own right." — Manning & Massumi, Thought in the Act Most of what we call "research" and most of what we call "creative practice" assume they are separate, sequential, activities. Research produces knowledge. Then, practice produces work. The knowledge informs the work. The work illustrates the knowledge. This is the typical “institutional model” of knowledge production. It is also the model we're going to spend the rest of this course systematically inhabiting and turning.Research-creation, as described by the authors Manning & Massumi is an activity that occurs at what they call the prebifurcation point : the point just before research and creation diverge into the institutional structures that evaluate them by separate criteria. At that point, making and thinking are not distinct acts. They are two registers of the same act, happening simultaneously.The theme of Week 01 is "Practice Immanent Critique." Here's what that phrase means from the ground up.An immanent critique does not stand outside a system to pass judgment. Instead, it works from inside. Id does so in order to inhabit the structure, understand its logic from within, and then find the pressure points where it might be turned. Manning & Massumi's definition:"An immanent critique engages with new processes more than new products, from a constructivist angle. It seeks to energize new modes of activity, already in germ, that seem to offer a potential to escape or overspill ready-made channelings into the dominant value system. The strategy of immanent critique is to inhabit one's complicity and make it turn — in the sense in which butter 'turns' to curd."Notice what this requires: inhabiting complicity. You are not exempt from the system you critique. You work from within it, on its tools, in its institutions, using its grants and its grades. Immanent critique means doing that while turning it, not waiting until you're free of it to begin this form of practice.So, let’s analyze this from our shared perspective. For this course: We are working at a university. We use tools (TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, Ableton, Python) that carry embedded worldviews. We receive grades. All of this is our complicity. Immanent critique is the method by which we make that complicity productive rather than just reproductive.Manning & Massumi acknowledge a tension: the institutional framing of research-creation — especially in the context of digital media and media studies — pushes it toward "formatting artistic activity for more directly economic forms of delivery to stakeholders." Digital media works often get funded in part because they "employ the same technological platforms as the increasingly computerized economy."For us, this is a friction of our practice (and a contradiction that is not easily resolved). Our work is to neither ignore this friction nor be paralyzed by it. Instead we should treat it as what Agre would call a hassle: a recurring friction that is itself data about the structure of the field.The danger Manning & Massumi identify: research-creation "settles into a communication model revolving around the delivery of results." The goal instead is what they call "an interpenetration of processes rather than a communication of products."What does that mean in practice? When you work on a project in this course, you are not primarily building something that will be assessed. You are practicing something. Developing a relationship to your tools, your materials, and your questions. The artifact becomes secondary, it is the record of that practice, not the point of it.These are technically different acts. Framing is setting up a structure: here are the rules, here are the constraints, here is the question, go. Conditioning is bringing co-causes into interaction such that something emerges that neither cause alone would produce. "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone… Emergent process, dedicated to the singular occurrence of the new, agitates inventively in an open field. Programmed organization, on the other hand, functions predictably in a bounded frame and lends itself to reproduction."In this class, we are going to try to condition rather than frame. We should strive to set up initial conditions; not attempt to predetermine outcomes.The concept that connects it all: enabling constraints.An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect even though it may be limiting in its form. The classic example: gravity is a constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Without gravity to push against, there is no arc, no lift, no landing. The jump is a collaboration between the dancer and gravity — two co-causes whose interaction produces something neither does alone."In our experience, unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects."This applies directly to the hardware and software in this course. The MPR121 sensor constrains what counts as input. CircuitPython constrains what you can compute on the microcontroller. OSC protocol constrains the format of the data. These are not obstacles — they are the material conditions out of which something emerges. The question is not how to eliminate constraints but how to turn them from limitative to enabling.Manning & Massumi introduce the concept of techniques of relation: "devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction" that comprise "a domain of practice in their own right." Techniques of relation are are structural: they shape how things interact, how processes co-evolve, how different elements of a practice can be brought into productive contact. They operate in two modes: Techniques that set up initial conditions — propitious starting points for emergence Techniques that modulate an event as it moves through its phases — improvised steering without predetermined destination A key property: "Techniques as we understand them do not depend exclusively on the content of the practices but move across their respective processes at the site of their potential multiplication." A technique is transferable. It can move from sound to movement to code to pedagogy.Assignment connection: Part of your ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal) practice is to identify the techniques of relation already operating in your practice in order to begin consciously designing new ones.If every practice is already a mode of thought, what is your current practice thinking?Manning & Massumi open Thought in the Act with: "Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act. To dance: a thinking in movement. To paint: a thinking through color. To perceive in the everyday: a thinking of the world's varied ways of affording itself."So for us: To program is a thinking in what? To route audio signals is a thinking in what? To touch a capacitive sensor is a thinking in what? To capture field recordings is a thinking in what? Right now, these are more rhetorical questions, but your first journal entries will begin to answer them, literally. Research-creation — activity at the prebifurcation point where making and thinking are co-constitutive, not sequential Immanent critique — inhabiting complicity and making it turn; critique from inside, not outside Enabling constraint — a limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction Conditioning — bringing co-causes into interaction toward open, emergent outcomes (vs. framing toward predetermined ones) Techniques of relation — devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction; transferable across practices

Failure as MethodDIGM 553 - W01A - Research-Creation as Method "Instruments have a life of their own. They do not merely follow theory; often they determine theory, because instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." — Hankins & Silverman, quoted in Magnusson
If W01Aestablished research-creation as the methodological orientation of this course, This section (W01B) establishes the epistemic status of the tools you work with.These two moves are connected: if making is already a mode of thinking, then the instrument you make with is already shaping the kinds of thought that are possible.This is what Magnusson, following Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, means by epistemic tools: instruments are not passive, nor neutral. Instruments (artistic, musical, scientific, or otherwise) act as active participants in the construction of knowledge. The choice of what instrument to use is also not neutral. It conditions what questions you can ask, what results you can produce, and, eventually, what can be considered beautiful, interesting, or true.For us, this puts our tool choices in a new light. Choosing TouchDesigner over Processing, Max/MSP over SuperCollider, a capacitive sensor over a camera are all epistemological decisions as much as they are technical ones.Don Ihde identified four phenomenological modalities of instrument-use. We will look at the three most prominent ways that instruments mediate between the body and the world:You act through the instrument, which extends your body or amplifies your senses. The instrument recedes into the background (the hidden 4th relation - Background Relations). You experience through and with technology, not at a technology. A well-practiced keyboard player doesn't think about the keys; they think about the music. The keys are an extension of the hand.The instrument produces data that you must interpret. A spectrograph, a heat map, an oscilloscope reading. The instrument mediates reality by translating it into a representation via abstractions, but that representation requires interpretive work to become knowledge.The instrument becomes something you engage with for its own sake, as a “quasi-other”, a presence with its own agency. Virtual reality headsets, interactive installations, or a generative system that responds to you all produce this kind of relation.Important These modalities should not be considered exclusive categories. Think of them more as tendencies. Any given practice involves mixtures and oscillations between them. And they are not value-neutral: each modality shapes what you notice, what you miss, and what you expect the instrument to do for you. One of Don Ihde's most directly practical insight: every instrument involves amplification-reduction transformations. It amplifies certain features of the world and reduces others. And there is no exception to this.One important question to always ask of a tool, technology, or model is: “What is gained and what is lost when I apply it?” A microphone (through a purely physical model/definition) amplifies pressure-wave events in a certain frequency ranges (based on it circuit design and construction) and reduces everything else. A MIDI controller amplifies discrete pitch/velocity events and reduces continuous, gestural sound. A capacitive touch sensor amplifies conductivity at specific points and reduces everything that isn't electrical contact. The danger is not that [tools/technologies/models/definitions] reduce. All of them do to some extent. The danger is forgetting that they do. When the reduction becomes invisible, the thing not being captured disappears from your thinking entirely.Magnusson on software: Musical software encodes inherited defaults: equal-tempered tuning, temporal quantization, note-based event models. But they aren’t musical “facts” or “truths” and they seldom capture the full range of musical expression. What they are contingent historical choices that have been naturalized through adoption (sometimes forced) and repeated use in which what was reduced has faded away. They have become what Latour (and Bowker & Star) call black boxes. A black box is an object or system whose internal workings have become invisible through repeated use. Latour: "objects establish themselves as black boxes through repeated use and in the process their origins disappear." Bowker and Star extend this: "the more naturalized the object becomes, the more unquestioning the relationship of the community to it; the more invisible the contingent and historical circumstances of its birth, the more it sinks into the community's routinely forgotten memory." Take note on what this means for practice: the tools you're most fluent with are the most dangerous. Fluency produces blindness. The instrument you've used for years is the instrument whose assumptions you've most thoroughly absorbed into your practice without noticing. Critical technical Practice (CTP) connection: This is why what Agre describes as the "split identity" matters. One foot in craft, one foot in critique. The craft foot needs fluency. The critique foot needs to keep opening the black boxes that fluency keeps closing.Philip Agre's phrase points to a specific version of “computational imperialism”: computers "aim to reinvent virtually every other site of practice in its own image." They are built from representational models and abstractions of the activities they will be used to perform. However, in doing so, But they also restructure those activities, fundamentally. Example A digital audio workstation (DAW) doesn't just record and edit audio. It restructures the practice of making music around the concept of a timeline, discrete regions, channels, effects chains, automation curves, etc… This perpetuates a model of music-making built by engineers with particular assumptions about what music is. A computer, then, does not simply have an instrumental use in a given site of practice; the computer is frequently about that site in its very design.This is why Agre says that technical people often experience phenomenological texts as "sounding like mysticism." The mismatch in philosophy and understanding exists because the computer's representational model and the phenomenologist's model of experience are genuinely incommensurable. You can't translate one into the other because they aren't the same kind of thing. Agre's solution: stop translating, start learning on their (meaning models and practice of phenomenological experiences) own terms.Thor Magnusson in ‘‘Sonic Writing” spins a particular historical framing of a driving problem this way: Western philosophy has long separated techne (making, craft, technique) from episteme (knowledge, theory, science). Instruments of art were not instruments of knowledge; skill was not wisdom.In more modern theory and practice, this separation is now being productively challenged: by cognitive science (embodied cognition, enactivism) by STS (Science and Technology Studies) by research-creation methodology by practitioners in new interfaces for musical expression, interactive art, and critical making. IN doing so, our instruments become epistemic, fusing instrument with composition, as in the works of Gordon Mumma, David Tudor, and other practitioners and disciplines. The digital system is, as Magnusson puts it, "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three registers are active all at once.Three questions to hold as you work through this course:What does your tool amplify? What aspects of your practice does it make easier to see, hear, measure, or manipulate? What does your tool reduce? What is systematically missing from what your tool captures? What can't it represent How has the above shaped what you've been making? Who designed the magnification-reduction? The defaults in your software were chosen by someone with specific assumptions. What were those assumptions, and whose experience of the world did they take as universally applicable? Epistemic tool — an instrument that is a knowledge-making artifact; tools determine what is possible and thus what can be thought Embodiment / hermeneutic / alterity relations — Ihde's three phenomenological modalities of instrument-world relationship Amplification-reduction — every tool amplifies certain features and reduces others; no tool is neutral (Ihde) Black box — a naturalized object whose internal contingency has become invisible through repeated use (Latour, Bowker & Star) Computational imperialism — the tendency of computing to reinvent every site of practice in its own representational image (Agre) Techne / episteme — the historically-separated domains of craft-knowledge and theoretical-knowledge, now being rejoined

A daily practice of noticing, logging, and analyzing friction points in your workflow is itself a research practice. → See ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal): structured hassle-logging is the assignment.🔴 Theory — Intermediation: Agre developed a vocabulary of concepts at "intermediate" levels of abstraction — neither fully phenomenological nor fully computational — that could function as the bridge between lived experience and technical specification.🟢 Pedagogic — Pattern recognition as technique: "As my intuitive understanding of the workings of everyday life evolved, I would formulate new concepts and intermediate on them, whereupon the resulting spontaneous observations would push my understanding of everyday life even further away from the concepts that I had been taught." Intermediation is a loop, not a translation.🟢 Pedagogic — THE lesson (Agre's breakthrough): "My first intellectual breakthrough came when, for reasons I do not recall, it finally occurred to me to stop translating these strange disciplinary languages into technical schemata, and instead simply to learn them on their own terms." This is how the empathize step in design should work — not projecting your framework onto another practice, but genuinely inhabiting its logic.🔴 Theory — Phenomenological texts as mysticism: "Many technical people have observed that phenomenological texts, when read as specifications for technical mechanisms, sound like mysticism." The problem is the reading mode, not the texts. Change the mode — stop looking for specs, start learning the vocabulary.🔴 Theory — Failure as method: "The intellectual utility of technical exercises, as distinct from the practical utility that they might actually have in the world, lies precisely in their limitations and failures." A failed system reveals its own design assumptions. What a system cannot do exposes what it assumed the world was.🟢 Pedagogic — Even incomplete work has value: Projects that don't meet their creators' expectations are not abject failures — "each of them introduced technical methods that may have some lasting value." But the work can only speak with "the rigor and insight with which it struggles against the patterns of difficulty that are inherent in its design."🔴 Theory — Four difficulties of CTP: Becoming aware of assumptions beneath existing practices Reducing a new intuition to a novel technical method Preventing new methods from being absorbed back into old schemata Applying new methods to real cases without reintroducing old scaffolding 🔴 Theory — THE KEY LESSON: "A critical technical practice will, at least for the foreseeable future, require a split identity — one foot planted in the craft work of design and the other foot planted in the reflexive work of critique."🟢 Pedagogic — Sitting with discomfort: "It will require a praxis of daily work: forms of language, career strategies, and social networks that support the exploration of alternative work practices that will inevitably seem strange to insiders and outsiders alike. This strangeness will not always be comfortable, but it will be productive nonetheless."🔵 Project Hook — CTP as goal for digital media: Critical practice aims at "complex engagement, not a clean break." You don't get to stand outside computation and critique it from purity. You build and critique simultaneously. The dissertation, the sculpture, the class project — all are sites where this split identity is practiced.🔴 Theory — Foucault on opposing schools: Via Foucault: "rather than try to adjudicate the dispute, one should investigate whether the opposed schools are internally related components of a single intellectual formation." The "computation vs. phenomenology" fight reveals that both operate inside the same formation — which is the insight that opens CTP. Identify a hassle in your current practice. Not a one-time frustration — a recurring pattern of friction. What does it tell you about the assumptions built into the tool causing it? Agre says his breakthrough was learning phenomenology on its own terms, not as a spec. What discipline outside your own have you tried to learn that way? What happened? What would "split identity" look like in your specific practice? What does the craft foot know that the critique foot doesn't, and vice versa? Agre says critics are often asked "what's your alternative?" within rules that "virtually rule out alternatives from the start." How do you propose an alternative without getting absorbed back into the existing schema? If tools "reinvent every site in their own image," what does your current software stack say the world is? Agre — Critical Technical Practice"Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act. To dance: a thinking in movement. To paint: a thinking through color." — Manning & MassumiWhat is your current practice thinking?Manning, E. & Massumi, B. (2014). Thought in the Act: Passages in the Ecology of Experience. University of Minnesota Press. [Propositions 0–3, pp. 83–94]
Assigned: Week 1, Week 2 🔴 Red = Core theoretical concept 🔵 Blue = Project / practice hook 🟢 Green = Pedagogic moment 🔴 Theory — Prebifurcation point: Research-creation occurs "at the constitutive level of both art practice and theoretical research, at a point before research and creation diverge into the institutional structures that capture and contain their productivity." At that point, making is already thinking-in-action, and conceptualization is a practice in its own right. The two intersect in technique.🔴 Theory — Techniques of emergence: "This idea of research-creation as embodying techniques of emergence takes it seriously that a creative art or design practice launches concepts-in-the-making." These concepts are mobile at the level of the techniques they continue to invent — the work is "as speculative (future-event oriented) as it is pragmatic (technique-based practice)."🟢 Pedagogic — Process vs. product: Manning & Massumi warn against research-creation settling "into a communication model revolving around the delivery of results." The goal is "an interpenetration of processes rather than a communication of products." This is the central caution for how to approach studio practice in this course.🟢 Pedagogic — Openness as condition: "The term 'research-creation' was retained as a key term for an exploratory openness in this activity of producing new modes of thought and action." R-C must be open-ended, not pre-programmed. Outcomes are "experimental, emergent effects of an ongoing process."🔴 Theory — Definition: "An immanent critique engages with new processes more than new products, from a constructivist angle. It seeks to energize new modes of activity, already in germ, that seem to offer a potential to escape or overspill ready-made channelings into the dominant value system. The strategy of immanent critique is to inhabit one's complicity and make it turn—in the sense in which butter 'turns' to curd."🔴 Theory — Built-in contradiction: Manning & Massumi note that neoliberal framing pushes research-creation toward "formatting artistic activity for more directly economic forms of delivery to stakeholders." Digital media sits in this exactly — "digital media began to take funding priority over traditional forms" partly because they "employ the same technological platforms as the increasingly computerized economy." This is an impasse, in the sense of Agre's hassle.🟢 Pedagogic — Institutional critique is personal: DJ's note: Drexel-style "interdisciplinary" work where disciplines "continue to work in their own institutional corners much as before, meeting only at the level of research results" is precisely what research-creation must resist. The course structure itself is an attempt to condition otherwise.🔴 Theory — Definition: "An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect, even though it may be limiting in its form/force narrowly considered."🔴 Theory — Conditioning vs. framing: "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone… Emergent process, dedicated to the singular occurrence of the new, agitates inventively in an open field. Programmed organization, on the other hand, functions predictably in a bounded frame and lends itself to reproduction."🔵 Project Hook — Gravity/dance example: The jump: gravity is implaccable, but add horizontal movement and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." Gravity converts from limitative to enabling constraint. → What is the "gravity" in your media system? The hardware constraints, the protocol limitations, the material resistance of your chosen tools?🟢 Pedagogic — Assignment connection: Students will design their own "techniques of relation — devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction." These techniques must "implant opportunities for creative participation, which would be encouraged to take on their own shape, direction, and momentum." → Links directly to ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal) and ASN 3 (Experimental Media Project).🔴 Theory — Two kinds of technique: Techniques to set in place propitious initial conditions Techniques to modulate the event as it moves through its phases 🔵 Project Hook — Techniques are agnostic: "Techniques as we understand them do not depend exclusively on the content of the practices but move across their respective processes at the site of their potential multiplication." → This gives students permission to borrow techniques across disciplines.🔴 Theory — Technique as passage: "A technique involves activating a passage between creative forces." It involves "practiced repetition and intensive exchange." Play and experimentation extend this.🟢 Pedagogic — Class as event: "For an 'event' to be an event, it is necessary that a collective thinking process be enacted that can give rise to new thoughts through the interaction on site. It is equally important that potential for what might occur not be pre-reduced to the delivery of already-arrived-at conclusions." → Approach seminar sessions this way.🔵 Project Hook — Co-causal thirdness: "Each of our events seeks collectively to find modalities of experimentation that connect practices at the levels of their intensive creative force. This is done not in order to map them onto one another, or to evaluate one in terms of another, but to propose a co-causal thirdness of exploration that can be generative of new modes of practice and inquiry." → The course as a whole is this kind of event. Manning & Massumi say research-creation happens "before research and creation diverge." What does that mean for how you currently describe your practice? Where do you typically put the boundary? What's the difference between framing a project and conditioning one? Think of a project you've done and ask: was it framed or conditioned? What enabling constraints are already active in your tools, materials, and methods — and which ones do you want to bring into play deliberately? "Unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects." Do you agree? What's the minimum constraint needed for something interesting to happen? How does your institution (Drexel, your discipline) shape what "results" your work is supposed to produce? How can immanent critique operate from inside that? Manning + Massumi — Thought in the ActMagnusson, T. (2019). 'Epistemic Tools.' In Sonic Writing: Technologies of Material, Symbolic, and Signal Inscriptions. Bloomsbury Academic. [Ch. 3, selected sections]
Assigned: Week 1, Week 2 🔴 Red = Core theoretical concept    🔵 Blue = Project / practice hook    🟢 Green = Pedagogic moment 🔴 Theory — Foundational claim (Hankins & Silverman): "Instruments have a life of their own. They do not merely follow theory; often they determine theory, because instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." This is the core argument for the concept of epistemic tools — the tool is not neutral; it is an epistemic artifact, carrying a worldview into every act of use.🟢 Pedagogic — Course hardware rationale: Why do we use specific hardware in this course rather than staying entirely in software? Because the choice of instrument conditions what kinds of thinking and making are possible. The MPR121 capacitive touch sensor does not "just" detect touch — it frames touch as a particular kind of data. The Zoom H5 does not "just" record — it frames sound as a particular kind of capture.🔴 Theory — Three modalities of instrument relation (Ihde 1990): Embodiment relations: the instrument extends the body or amplifies the senses (we act through it) Hermeneutic relations: the instrument provides data we must interpret — like a spectrograph or heat map Alterity relations: the technology becomes something we engage with for its own sake — virtual reality, for instance, or a musical instrument that plays back 🔵 Project Hook — Entangled modalities: These relations are "not in isolation from one another, but are themselves an entangled web/knot." A single session working with TouchDesigner and a sensor involves all three simultaneously — you act through it (embodiment), read its outputs (hermeneutic), and sometimes play with it as its own thing (alterity). The task is to notice which mode is active and when.🔴 Theory — No neutral tool (Ihde 1979): "Technology equally conceals and reveals… Technologies organise, select, focus the task, and shape the environment through various transformations. This is what Ihde calls amplification-reduction transformations." Every tool amplifies certain features of the world and reduces others. There is no tool that is neutral.🔵 Project Hook — Inherited defaults as worldviews: Musical software carries embedded assumptions: "halftone equal tempered tuning, temporal quantisation, or note-based event model." These are not inevitable features of music — they are contingent historical choices now naturalized into default. → What defaults has your current software stack inherited? Which do you accept, which do you resist?🟢 Pedagogic — Tool critique is practice critique: "We must become critically aware of, navigate, and refute (become fugitives) when we pick and utilize certain tools. We must not subconsciously and unknowingly continue to present certain worldviews if they are not aligned with our being." This is not about avoiding tools — it is about practicing with a critical awareness of what they bring.🔴 Theory — Naturalization (Latour / Bowker & Star): "Objects establish themselves as black boxes through repeated use and in the process their origins disappear. The object is naturalised through heavy use, a fact prompting Bowker and Star to observe that the 'more naturalized the object becomes, the more unquestioning the relationship of the community to it; the more invisible the contingent and historical circumstances of its birth, the more it sinks into the community's routinely forgotten memory.'"🟢 Pedagogic — Black-boxing as danger: The danger is not complexity — it's forgetting. When we forget that a tool is a contingent artifact, we stop questioning it. CTP (Agre) and research-creation (Manning & Massumi) are both, in part, practices of deliberately opening black boxes back up.🔴 Theory — The separation and its questioning: "If the problem of Western philosophy has been the separation of techne and episteme, this dichotomy is now being questioned, following a better understanding in cognitive science and the role of active perception." The early modern conception: instruments are "containers of theory" — the musician engages with a system of thought when performing on an instrument.🔴 Theory — Three modes of epistemological work (Baird): Model knowledge: the instrument as material mode of representation Working knowledge: the instrument as mode of effective action Encapsulated knowledge: the instrument synthesizing representation and action together "Technological artefacts are models of thought, performing epistemological work alongside scientific theories, and often preceding them."🟢 Pedagogic — The historical question: When did instruments of the arts lose their epistemic status? When did the art instrument cease to be studied as a knowledge-making device? The interdisciplinary turn is, in part, a recovery of that status.🔴 Theory — Material / electric / symbolic: "The digital system is material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." Unlike acoustic instruments, where most time with the instrument does not involve symbolic thought, digital instruments are fundamentally representational. "Behind our simple instrument are layers of microchips, busses, memory; operating systems, code libraries, classes; protocols, standards."🔵 Project Hook — Designer decides: "The designer decides what is revealed and what is concealed when the system is used." When the designer is also the performer, the researcher, and the observer — as in autoethnographic research practice — navigating these roles requires deliberate switching.🔵 Project Hook — Play as modality: "In music technologies, this manifests through play, through playing the instrument, but also the playful interaction that can emerge between a human and machine if the latter is given agency." The question of machine agency — explored in Somax2, in generative systems, in AI improvisation — is precisely the question of what kind of play becomes possible when the instrument pushes back. Pick one tool you use daily. What does it amplify about your practice? What does it reduce or make invisible? Magnusson says the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, symbolic in control." What does the "symbolic" layer of your tool hide about the material layer underneath? Ihde describes embodiment, hermeneutic, and alterity relations with instruments. Which of these dominates your current hardware/software setup, and why? What in your current stack is a black box you've stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened it? Hankins & Silverman say tools determine theory. What theory is being determined by the specific hardware we're using in this course? Magnusson — Epistemic Tools

As data continues to permeate all aspects of our lives, the need for datafluency becomes paramount. The "Data Shed" project explores the intersectionof interactive art, machine learning, and data visualization to facilitate experien-tial learning about data and its pervasive influence in our digital age. Groundedin the metaphor of shedding, akin to a snake's skin, the installation portrays theimplicit generation and shedding of latent data in our digital interactions. Thepaper delves into related work, emphasizing the accelerating role of algorithms,motivated by the challenges posed by data misuse and potential for bias. It drawson the concepts of data fluency and critical data studies, exploring the paradox ofprivacy in the face of increasing concerns about data handling by organizations.The study reviews generative artworks and human-AI collaboration before ad-dressing the ability of machine learning to address surveillance and data-shed-ding concerns. The paper details research creation, the development methodol-ogy, and highlights gaps where the "Data Shed" approach can bring focus to theseissues. Evaluative insights are provided, emphasizing technical goals, interactiv-ity levels, and assessment of achievement of data fluency objectives. The re-search underscores the importance of interactive art works, user engagement, andethical considerations, in fostering a deeper understanding of data in our digitallandscape. The project invites users to reflect on the shaping influence of data inour lives and its potential impact on our collective future.Keywords: Data Collection, Data Ownership, Latent Data, Data Shedding, Ma-chine Learning, Generative Art, Interactive Installation.1 IntroductionThe interactive art installation, “Data Shed,” is designed to facilitate understanding andexperiential learning about data. It conceptualizes data shedding as a “natural” process,drawing an analogy from the shedding of a snake's skin. This representation capturesthe implicit generation and shedding of latent data in our digital interactions. Data shed-ding occurs in various interactions with technology or even when we are near it, fromlocation tracking, sensor systems, facial recognition, search engines, to online shop-ping.As data has become ubiquitous in our lives; data are all around us, and we constantlygenerate data without even realizing it. The rapid progress in artificial intelligence andmachine learning, fueled by data, has given rise to new algorithms and technologies
that are accelerated by the rapid breakthroughs in the field. Despite having all these2 A. Verma et al.data and access to powerful tools we understand so little about how data is collectedand how data directs our decisions and choices in this well woven digital environmentand economy. Data fluency is the key to unlocking knowledge and understanding howdata has become the main ingredient of the digital age.1Data are used to make many of our day-to-day activities easier. For instance, a per-son purchasing a transit ticket in many places around the world provides the data fromthe station they are boarding and the destination station. The data trade-off gives in-sights such as identifying the stations that see higher footfall, which can then be usedto design stations and transit schedules, responding to the footfall at different stations.This is an example of how a small interaction can lead to data generation in an implicitmanner, where the users are not aware they generated data through their interactions.These examples can be described as latent data that exists around the user withoutthem knowing about it.As more organizations start collecting personal data, there is a growing need forpeople to understand this hidden force acting on their behalf, making decisions forthem, and how all this data is being collected with the use of new algorithmic systems.Given this context it is essential for us to seek more ethical and conscientious meth-ods of utilizing the vast amount of data collected. “Data Shed” fills this gap inknowledge by actively addressing the imperative for ethical data practices. “Data Shed”responds to the call for ethical data practices by empowering users with insights intothe often-unnoticed world of data shedding, thereby contributing to a more informedand responsible approach to data utilization.2 Related WorkThe literature review draws on a wide range of sources, including studies on data col-lection, algorithmic bias, and critical data studies to form the foundation for understand-ing the multifaceted landscape of data in our digital age. The exploration extends to therise of machine learning, addressing concerns related to surveillance and data shedding.Related work includes generative artworks and human-AI collaboration, contributingto the theoretical groundwork for understanding the intersections of technology, art,and data. This theoretical framework forms the backdrop against which the "Data Shed"project unfolds.2.1 Navigating Data's Dominance in the Modern Age: Algorithms,Acceleration and Data shedding Dynamics.In the past decade, the world has seen a tremendous increase in the use of artificialintelligence (AI). AI systems are evolving so fast that it has become increasingly pos-sible to build an intelligent computer system that is programmed to do a single task. See Readings for full citations.Week 11Spring 2026A map of the course's entanglements — weeks and their conceptual threads.BEGINENDThe methodology holding critical inquiry, technical exploration, and creative production together as co-constitutive practices — not sequential phases, but registers of the same act.Manning & Massumi locate research-creation at the prebifurcation point: the moment before thinking and making diverge into separate institutional structures. At that point, making is already thinking-in-action, and conceptualization is a practice in its own right. The problem research-creation names — and refuses — is the communication model: the assumption that you research first, then make something that delivers the results.The alternative is conditioning over framing. Rather than setting up a question and then answering it, you bring co-causes into interaction and stay open to what emerges. This requires what Manning & Massumi call techniques of relation — structural devices for catalyzing interaction between forces that wouldn't otherwise meet. They are not content-specific; they transfer across disciplines and practices.For this course, the implication is practical: the Critical Technical Journal is not documentation of a separate making process. The making is not an illustration of the thinking. They interpenetrate — or the work isn't research-creation.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10, Week 11 Where in your workflow do making and thinking happen in the same moment — not sequentially, but simultaneously? Can you locate that moment and work from it deliberately? What would it mean for your project to be conditioned rather than framed? What are you holding open, and what are you predetermining? If you had to say what your practice is thinking right now — not what you're making, but what the act of making is already processing — what would you say? What institutional structures (program requirements, evaluation criteria, submission formats) separate your thinking from your making? How do you work inside those structures without simply reproducing them?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — the foundational text. Propositions 0–3 define research-creation, enabling constraints, and techniques of relation.
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on curiosity as a legitimate research methodology; what it means to follow a question rather than test a hypothesis.
Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Making PublicResearch-CreationTools are not neutral. Every instrument encodes a worldview — a set of propositions about what the world is, what can be known about it, and who that knowledge is for.Magnusson, drawing on Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, argues that instruments don't merely follow theory — they often determine it, because "instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." An epistemic tool is any instrument understood this way: as a knowledge-making artifact with its own claims built in.Ihde identifies three modalities of how instruments mediate between body and world: embodiment relations (you act through the tool, which recedes), hermeneutic relations (the tool produces data you must interpret), and alterity relations (you engage with the tool as a quasi-other). These aren't fixed categories — any practice oscillates between them, and the shift matters.Every tool also performs an amplification-reduction: it amplifies certain features of the world and systematically reduces others. The danger isn't reduction itself — all tools must reduce. The danger is when the reduction becomes invisible, when it gets naturalized into what Latour calls a black box: an object whose internal contingency has disappeared through repeated use. Fluency closes black boxes. The critique foot of Agre's split identity keeps reopening them.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5 What does your primary tool amplify — what becomes easy, visible, measurable? And what does it reduce — what disappears, gets rounded off, or can't be represented? Who designed the defaults in your software? What assumptions about bodies, practices, and contexts are baked into those choices? Which of Ihde's three modalities describes your relationship to your tool right now? When does it shift — and what triggers the shift? What's the most naturalized tool in your practice — the one you've stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened that black box?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — the source text for the concept; covers Ihde's modalities, amplification-reduction, and the techne/episteme distinction.
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — on computational imperialism, the split identity, and the practice of making the invisible assumptions of tools visible.
Research-Creation   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as MethodEpistemic ToolsA limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction. The paradox at the heart of creative practice: the right constraint doesn't close things down — it opens them.Manning & Massumi's example: gravity is an implacable constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Add horizontal momentum, and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." Remove gravity and there's no arc — no lift, no landing, no jump as an event. The constraint is generative because of its resistance, not despite it.The enabling constraint is how this course thinks about everything from protocol choices to assignment structures. The MPR121 sensor's 12-point reduction is a constraint; it enables a certain kind of sculptural thinking. OSC over UDP dropping packets is a constraint; it forces a real-time compositional response to instability. The 3-hour seminar session is a constraint; it enables a depth of engagement that 50-minute sessions preclude.The critical move: distinguishing a constraint that merely limits from one that enables. Manning & Massumi: "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone." An enabling constraint is always a co-cause — it only becomes enabling in relation to something else it can push against.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 8 What in your practice functions as gravity — the implacable resistance you push against? Is it enabling or merely limitative? What would it take to make it enabling? What's the difference between a rule you've been given and a constraint you've designed? Have you ever designed a constraint for yourself that actually worked? When you hit a wall in a project, is it usually a limitative constraint (stop here) or an enabling one (find the co-cause)? How do you tell the difference in the moment? What would it mean to design the constraints of your project before you design its content?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3; the concept of enabling constraints and conditioning is developed here in full.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Physical-Digital EntanglementEnabling ConstraintsPractitioner, tool, and material do not interact as pre-formed, separate entities. They are mutually constituted through the practice itself. You don't bring a self to a tool — the self that acts is partly made by the act.Barad's posthumanist performativity replaces interaction (between pre-existing things) with intra-action (the process through which distinct agencies emerge). An apparatus — for Barad, any material-discursive arrangement that makes knowledge possible — doesn't just measure or represent phenomena; it participates in producing them. The researcher, the instrument, and the phenomenon are all co-constituted through the apparatus.For this course, that means: you are not a stable subject using a neutral tool to study an external object. You are entangled with your hardware, your software, your materials, and the site of your practice. These entanglements are not metaphors — they are structural features of how knowledge gets made. Documenting them honestly is part of what the Critical Technical Journal is for.Camus & Vinck extend this into digital materiality: the digital is not immaterial. It is made of matter — servers, cables, electricity, screen light. Every "digital" thing has a thickness, a weight, a set of dependencies. The click is a material event. The file is an inscription on physical media. Recognizing this thickness is how you stop treating your tools as transparent windows onto some other reality.
Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What are you entangled with in your current project — not just using, but mutually constituted by? What would change about the project if that entanglement changed? Barad replaces "interaction" with "intra-action." What's the difference? Try to locate an intra-action — a moment where the boundaries between you, your tool, and your material were genuinely unclear. Where does the "digital" in your practice have material weight — consume power, require infrastructure, produce heat, leave traces? If your apparatus (the whole material-discursive arrangement of your practice) is not just measuring phenomena but helping produce them — what phenomena is yours producing?
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness of digital objects; the materiality of inscription and infrastructure.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — the concept of co-causality and conditioning is entanglement in practice.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as MethodEntanglementFailure and impasse are not obstacles to the project. They are data about the project — revealing the formative conditions, hidden assumptions, and structural tensions that define what the work is actually doing.Agre's concept of the hassle is foundational here: not a one-time crash, but a recurring friction — something that keeps happening at the same point in your workflow, for reasons you can't quite name. Hassles are worth writing down. They are the system telling you something structural about the gap between how your tool models the world and how the world actually works.The move Agre names — and this course practices — is to treat impasse as an intellectual resource. When something fails repeatedly, don't just fix it and move on. Ask: what assumption was I making that this failure is disconfirming? What was I treating as settled that isn't? These are the questions the Critical Technical Journal is built to hold.Manning & Massumi's concept of immanent critique is also relevant here: failure, encountered from inside the practice, reveals the pressure points of the system. You can't see those pressure points from outside. You find them by building, hitting walls, and noticing where the resistance is structural rather than incidental.
Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a one-off problem, but something that keeps coming back? What is that hassle about? What assumption does it keep bumping against? When you hit a dead end in a project, how do you usually respond? Do you route around it, sit with it, or abandon it? What would it look like to study it instead? What's the difference between a failure that tells you something and one that doesn't? How do you tell them apart in the moment? If you had to name your most productive creative failure — the one that most changed how you work — what would you call it? What intermediation term would Agre give it?
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — the source of the hassle concept and the method of treating recurring friction as intellectual data.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — immanent critique as the practice of finding pressure points from inside the system.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Collective PracticeFailure as MethodThe interweaving of physical materials, bodies, and environments with digital systems. Not an interface between two separate domains — an entanglement in which each shapes the other.The signal chain at the center of this course — body → sensor → microcontroller → protocol → software → output — is not a pipeline that converts physical reality into digital representation. It is a series of transformations, each of which amplifies something and reduces something else. The body that touches the capacitive sensor is not the same as the threshold-crossing event the sensor registers. The OSC message is not the gesture. Something is always gained; something is always lost. What matters is knowing which something — and making that choice deliberately.Magnusson: the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three layers are active at once. The hardware has physical affordances that shape how you hold it, where you put it, what it can touch. The firmware has temporal properties that shape the resolution and latency of the response. The software has representational assumptions that shape what the data means. None of these layers is neutral; together they constitute the instrument.This thread tracks how physical and digital forces meet, condition each other, and produce something neither could alone — across your hardware choices, your material selections, your installation environments, and your audience's bodies.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10 At each arrow in your signal chain, what is being amplified and what is being reduced? Is that tradeoff intentional — a design decision — or accidental? What does your system not know about the body it's sensing? And what creative or critical work can happen in that gap? Where in your practice does the physical environment shape the digital behavior — and vice versa? Can you design the entanglement rather than just inheriting it? What material are you touching with your sensors or microcontrollers? What cultural, social, or political charge does that material carry — and does your system acknowledge it?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — on instruments as material-electric-symbolic systems and the phenomenology of digital tool relations.
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness and materiality of digital objects; the matter-network.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   EntanglementPhysical-Digital EntanglementRendering work public is not the delivery of results. It is a continuation of the research — a way of making the formative conditions and processual transformation of the work available for encounter.Loveless, working through Haraway, argues that research-creation carries an obligation to render research public — not as a finished product submitted to evaluation, but as a practice in itself. What gets made public is not just the artifact but the forces that formed it: the impasses, the enabling constraints, the entanglements, the tools and their reductions. This is why the Final Presentation in this course is not a showcase. It is a rendering.The distinction Loveless makes is between transparency (showing your work) and accountability (taking responsibility for what your work does in the world — including what it can't do, what it excludes, and who it speaks to or past). Accountability requires knowing the stakes of the work, not just the process.For experimental media practice, making public also means confronting the question of audience: who is this for? What does it ask of the people who encounter it? A TouchDesigner patch sent to a hard drive is not public; the same patch running in a gallery space with bodies moving through it is. The difference is not technical. It is relational — and designing that relation is itself a creative and ethical act.
Week 6, Week 9, Week 11 What would it mean to make your process public — not just your result? What would you have to show that you've been hiding? Who is the audience for your work, and what does it ask of them? Have you designed that ask, or inherited it from the format? Loveless distinguishes transparency from accountability. Where in your practice are you being transparent (showing your method) without being accountable (owning what the work does or fails to do)? What form is your work made public in, and what does that form assume about who can access it?
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on the obligation to render research public, curiosity as method, and the boundary object.
Research-Creation   Collective Practice   Failure as Method   EntanglementMaking PublicThe studio is not a collection of individual practices happening in parallel. It is a site of collective becoming — where techniques of relation between practitioners are themselves a subject of inquiry.Manning & Massumi describe the seminar or studio event as a kind of experiment: "For an 'event' to be an event, it is necessary that a collective thinking process be enacted that can give rise to new thoughts through the interaction on site." The condition: the potential for what might occur cannot be pre-reduced to "the delivery of already-arrived-at conclusions." This course is structured with that in mind. The critique, the potluck, the studio session — these are not performances of finished thinking. They are techniques of relation in the Manning & Massumi sense: devices for catalyzing interaction between practices at the level of their creative force.Critique, in this frame, is not judgment. It is activation — a practice of attending carefully to someone else's work in order to surface what it is doing that it may not know it's doing. A good critique question doesn't evaluate ("this works / this doesn't"). It opens ("what is this committed to? what does it refuse? what would it look like to follow that refusal further?").Collective practice also carries an ethic: you are responsible for what you bring to the room. Your presence, your attention, and your honest response to others' work are contributions to a shared intellectual environment. This is not a soft requirement. It is part of the assessment.
Week 2, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 11 What is the difference between a critique that evaluates and one that activates? What does an activating question sound like? What do you bring to the room as a practitioner that no one else does? What does the collective gain from your specific presence and perspective? When you encounter someone else's work in critique, what is your first instinct — to assess it, to identify with it, to question it? What would it mean to attend to it before doing any of those things? How does your practice change when it's in dialogue with others? What has a peer's question or response revealed to you about your own work?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — on the studio event as a site of collective thinking, and techniques of relation as a domain of practice.

Develop experimental digital media projects through a research-creation methodology that integrates critical inquiry, technical exploration, and creative production as co-constitutive practices. Recognize and articulate the entanglement of practitioner, tool, and material in the creative process. Design and iterate enabling constraints that guide the creative process without predetermining outcomes. gmap-395/guides/gmap-395-guide-ct-and-cp.title: GMAP 395 - Guide - CT and CPS
gmap-395/guides/gmap-395-guide-ct-and-cp.description:
In creative and technical work, the ability to solve problems systematically often matters more than any specific tool knowledge. Whether you're debugging a shader, designing a character, or optimizing game performance, the same core thinking skills apply.This guide teaches you to approach challenges methodically rather than hoping for inspiration or getting paralyzed by complexity. You'll learn to break down problems, research effectively, and iterate toward solutions.How This Connects: This guide pairs with the GMAP 395 - Guide - Procedural Modeling Fundamentals - the problem-solving framework here applies directly to technical modeling challenges, while working through geometry problems reinforces these thinking patterns. 🎯 Problem/Goal: You're tasked with creating an entire game environment but feel overwhelmed by the scope.Quick Reality Check, Ask yourself: "If I had to demo this in 2 weeks, what's the absolute minimum that needs to work?"Breaking It Down Step-by-Step Instead of: "I need to make a castle, fast" (panic mode) Try this: 🔴 Core: Outer walls + main gate + courtyard 🟡 Systems: Towers (3), inner buildings (2), details 🟢 Order: Blockout → structures → props → polish Common Pitfall Don't start with the most exciting part - start with what everything else depends on.🔽 **Top-Down** Layout → Major structures → Details → Polish 🔼 **Bottom-Up** Modular pieces → Combinations → Full system 👥 **Collaborative** Team brainstorm → Divide responsibilities → Regular check-ins Learn More
Environment Design Fundamentals
Game Production Pipelines
Scoping for Indie Games Apply this to shader creation: Break down realistic water material: 🔴 Core: Base color + basic normal 🟡 Systems: Waves + foam + reflection + refraction 🟢 Dependencies: Surface → animation → interaction effects Success Metric You've mastered this when you can take any overwhelming task and create a clear, ordered breakdown in under 30 minutes.🎯 Problem/Goal: Understanding what you're really working with and against so you can plan realistically.Design Wisdom "Constraints are not limitations - they're the foundation that makes creativity possible."Constraint-Driven Design Given: Mobile character with strict limits Constraints become features: Low poly → Stylized, iconic look Single texture → Cohesive color palette No transparency → Bold, graphic design Small screen → Strong silhouette focus 🎯 Constraint Prioritization: Rank which limits are hardest vs. most flexible 💡 Creative Reframing: Ask "What becomes possible because of this limitation?" 📊 Resource Auditing: List available tools, time, and skills Pro Technique Document your constraints visually - create a "constraint poster" for your workspace as a constant reminder.Apply constraint analysis to a UI design: Technical: Screen sizes, input methods, performance Usability: Accessibility, user experience, platform conventions Aesthetic: Brand guidelines, art direction, readability Success Metric You can quickly identify the 3 most limiting constraints for any project and explain how they'll shape your approach.🎯 Problem/Goal: You need to create something you've never made before and don't know where to start.Research Strategy in Action Goal: Cartoon-style water shader Research layers: 🎨 Visual: How does stylized water "read" as water? 🔧 Technical: What real-time techniques exist? 💭 Conceptual: How do animators suggest water movement? Reference Organization Create folders by project and concept Tag images with keywords and techniques Note why each reference is useful Share collections with team members 🖼️ Mood Boards: Feeling and atmosphere over technical specifics 🔧 Technical Breakdowns: Focus on construction methods 👥 Collaborative Research: Team members research different aspects Essential Resources
ArtStation Learning
80 Level Breakdowns
Real-Time Rendering Resources Research for character design across game genres: Visual: Art styles, proportions, appeal factors Technical: Rigging constraints, animation needs, performance Conceptual: Psychology of character design, cultural considerations Success Metric You can efficiently gather diverse, relevant references and explain how each one informs your creative decisions.🎯 Problem/Goal: The exact solution doesn't exist, but similar problems have been solved elsewhere.Translation Process Film technique: Complex particle systems Core principle: Layered depth creates visual richness Game adaptation: Animated texture layers with depth sorting Common Mistake Don't just copy techniques - understand why they work first. 🎯 Direct Adaptation: Recreate exactly, then optimize 💡 Principle Extraction: Understand the why, rebuild the how 🔄 Hybrid Methods: Combine multiple source approaches Cross-Pollination Technique Regularly browse fields outside your specialty - architecture, fashion, industrial design, biology.Adapt web design patterns to game UI: Hover effects → Controller/touch feedback Navigation patterns → Game menu systems Responsive design → Multiple screen sizes Success Metric You can see solutions in unexpected places and successfully adapt them to your creative challenges.🎯 Problem/Goal: Not all tutorials and advice are good - how do you know what to trust?Conflicting Advice Scenario Source A: "Never exceed 1,000 triangles" Source B: "Up to 5,000 triangles is fine" Source C: "It depends on your target device" Evaluation process:Validation Strategy Context Check: When, where, why was this advice given? Small Test: Build minimal example to verify claims Reasoning Analysis: Understand the underlying logic 👥 Community Validation: Ask experienced practitioners 🧪 Personal Testing: Build experiments to verify claims 📚 Contextual Research: Find advice specific to your situation Information Quality Red Flags No source attribution or credentials Claims without supporting evidence Advice that seems too good to be true Information that contradicts established best practices Evaluate design principles for different audiences: Research: What evidence supports these principles? Test: How do different user groups respond? Context: When do these principles apply vs. not apply? Success Metric You can quickly assess information credibility and know when to dig deeper vs. accept advice.🎯 Problem/Goal: You need to test ideas quickly without investing too much time in any single approach.Prototype Progression Week 1: Gray boxes, test jump feel Week 2: Basic character shape, test animations Week 3: Add visual feedback, test player reactions Week 4: Final art pass on proven mechanics Prototyping Hierarchy Core functionality (does it work?) User experience (does it feel right?) Visual polish (does it look good?) 📄 Paper Prototypes: Test concepts without digital tools 🖼️ Digital Mockups: Non-functional visual representations 🔧 Hybrid Methods: Combine low-fi and high-fi strategically Prototype Pitfalls Making prototypes too polished (wastes time) Testing only one variable at a time (misses interactions) Skipping documentation (loses valuable insights) Prototype a new art style: Visual test: Single character/prop in new style Consistency test: Multiple assets using same approach Context test: Assets in actual game environment Success Metric You can rapidly test core assumptions and pivot based on prototype feedback without emotional attachment to early work.🎯 Problem/Goal: Learning from your process so you can improve and repeat successes.Documentation Template Project: Stylized Water Shader Goal: Cartoon ocean for mobile game Research: 3 days studying animated films Attempts: Tried particle system (too heavy), vertex animation (wrong look) Breakthrough: Combined UV scrolling with vertex displacement Result: 60fps on target device, matches art style Next time: Start with performance constraints, not visual goals Documentation Timing During work: Quick notes, screenshots of progress After sessions: Reflection on what worked/didn't Project end: Complete analysis and lessons learned 📝 Written Logs: Traditional journaling and note-taking 📸 Visual Documentation: Screenshots, progress videos, annotated images 🎥 Process Recording: Screen capture while working Documentation Tools Text: Notion, Obsidian, simple markdown files Visual: Milanote, PureRef, Pinterest boards Mixed: Personal wiki, team knowledge base Document a challenging modeling or animation process: Process: What steps did you follow? Problems: Where did you get stuck and how did you solve it? Patterns: What problem-solving approaches emerged? Success Metric You have a growing personal knowledge base that you actively reference and update, making each project easier than the last.🎯 Problem/Goal: Getting help when stuck and explaining your work to others effectively.Poor vs. Good Help Requests ❌ Poor request: "My shader is broken, help!" ✅ Good request: "I'm creating a stylized water shader for mobile. It should look cartoon-like but I'm getting realistic results. Here's what I have [screenshot], here's what I want [reference image], and here's what I've tried [node graph]. Working in Blender 3.6, targeting Android devices. Any suggestions for the cartoon look?" 💬 Synchronous: Real-time conversation, screen sharing 📧 Asynchronous: Detailed written explanations with materials 🎥 Video: Record problem demonstration with narration Help Request Template Goal: What are you trying to achieve? Current State: What's happening now? Context: Tools, platform, constraints Attempts: What have you already tried? Specific Ask: What kind of help do you need? Explain a complex technical process to a non-technical team member: Use analogies and visual aids Focus on outcomes rather than methods Check understanding throughout explanation Success Metric You consistently get helpful responses to your questions and can explain your work clearly to different audiences.🎯 Problem/Goal: Accelerating your growth by understanding how others think through challenges.What to Look For Surface level: What tools they use, what settings they choose Deeper level: When they pause to evaluate, how they handle mistakes, what order they work in Deepest level: How they think about problems, what principles guide their decisions Active Learning Approach Watch once for overall impression Watch again taking notes on decision points Try to replicate the approach on your own project Adapt the method to your specific needs 🎓 Structured Learning: Courses, workshops, formal training 💬 Community Learning: Forums, Discord servers, study groups 🔍 Self-Directed Study: Analyzing published work and breakdowns Learning Communities
Polycount - Technical art community
Real-Time VFX - Effects artists
Tech Art Aid - Technical art resources Analyze a workflow from a different creative field: Architecture: How do architects plan complex projects? Film: How do VFX artists approach problem-solving? Product Design: How do industrial designers iterate? Adapt one insight to your game development work.Success Metric You can identify valuable learning opportunities in unexpected places and successfully integrate new approaches into your workflow.The techniques in this guide become more powerful with practice. Start applying them to small challenges before tackling major projects. Each problem you solve systematically builds your confidence and expands your toolkit.Key Takeaways Break down complex challenges into manageable pieces Research broadly and adapt solutions creatively Iterate quickly and learn from failures Document your process for future reference Collaborate effectively to amplify your capabilities Next Steps Practice these techniques on your current projects Build your personal reference and knowledge libraries Find communities where you can both seek and offer help Continue learning by analyzing others' problem-solving approaches Remember: The goal isn't to never get stuck, but to have systematic ways of getting unstuck. Every challenge becomes an opportunity to strengthen your problem-solving skills.

gmap-395/guides/gmap-395-guide-procedura.title: GMAP 395 - Guide - Procedural Modeling Fundamentals
gmap-395/guides/gmap-395-guide-procedura.description:
Procedural modeling means creating geometry through systematic, repeatable processes rather than manually placing every vertex. This approach excels in game development where you need efficient workflows, consistent results, and the ability to iterate quickly.This guide teaches modular thinking - breaking complex forms into simple, reusable components that combine into sophisticated systems. While examples use Blender's Geometry Nodes, these principles apply to any procedural modeling tool.How This Connects: This guide pairs with the Critical Thinking and Creative Problem-Solving - the systematic problem-solving approaches there apply directly to procedural modeling challenges, while working through geometry problems reinforces those thinking patterns. Example File 📁 Below is a link to download the blender file used for the short concept demo videos in this guide. It has all of the geometry nodes and obejcts labeled by chapter number i.e. 2.1 - Wall
procGenGuide.blend 🎯 Problem/Goal: When should you choose procedural approaches over traditional modeling?Key Decision Point Ask yourself: "Will I need multiple variations of this, or will it change frequently during development?"Building System Breakdown Manual approach: Model walls, roof, windows individually (3 days) Copy and modify for 5 variations (2 more days) Client wants changes (start over: 2+ days) Procedural approach: Define parameter system (4 days) Generate 50 variations (instant) Client changes (adjust parameters: hours) When to Choose Procedural ✅ Need multiple variations ✅ Expect frequent changes ✅ Repetitive patterns involved ✅ Performance optimization needed ❌ One-off hero assets ❌ Highly organic, unique forms ❌ Tight deadline with simple needs 🔧 Full Procedural: Everything generated from parameters 🎨 Template-Based: Manual base with procedural variations 🔄 Hybrid Workflow: Manual hero pieces, procedural background Essential Tools
Blender Geometry Nodes
Houdini
Maya MASH Identify procedural opportunities in your current project: What gets repeated with variations? What might change during development? Where do you spend time on repetitive tasks? Success Metric You can quickly evaluate whether a modeling task would benefit from procedural approaches and explain the trade-offs.🎯 Problem/Goal: Building complex systems from simple, reusable components.System Implementation Geometry Nodes hierarchy: Wall Component: length, height → wall geometry Building Component: uses walls, adds roof_type, door_count District Component: arranges buildings with spacing, variety Village Component: combines districts with roads and features Modular Design Principles Single Responsibility: Each component does one thing well Composability: Components combine in predictable ways Parameterization: Expose the right level of control Documentation: Clear naming and organization 🏗️ Hierarchical Systems: Clear levels of complexity 🕸️ Network Systems: Flexible component connections 📋 Template Systems: Pre-built arrangements with variation Modular Pitfalls Over-engineering simple tasks Creating too many parameters (analysis paralysis) Losing artistic control to systems Ignoring performance implications Apply modular thinking to non-geometry systems: UI System: Buttons → Panels → Screens → Full Interface Animation Rig: Controls → Sub-systems → Character → Scene Material Library: Textures → Shaders → Material Sets → Environment Success Metric You naturally think in terms of reusable components and can design systems that others can understand and extend.🎯 Problem/Goal: Understanding the building blocks of all geometry.Wall Component Setup In Geometry Nodes: Cube Primitive → base shape Transform: Scale X (length), Z (height), Y (thickness) Set Origin: Bottom center for ground placement (set position offset) Distribute Points on Faces: End faces for connections Instance Cubes: Small connection indicators
Concept Demo Video 📹 gmap395_g_pm_2.1.mp4 Transform Best Practices Consistent Origins: Decide on pivot standards for your project Parameter Ranges: Set min/max values that make sense Local vs. World: Understand coordinate system implications Non-Destructive: Keep original proportions accessible 📐 Mathematical Generation: Create primitives from formulas 📍 Point-Based Construction: Build from vertex positions 🎨 Profile-Based: Extrude shapes from 2D curves Geometry Nodes Primitives Cube - Basic box primitive Cylinder - Radial geometry Sphere - Subdivided sphere (UV or Icosphere) Grid - Plane with subdivisions Create modular primitives for specific art styles: Cyberpunk: Angular, tech-heavy base shapes Organic Forest: Curved, natural-form primitives Minimalist: Clean, simple geometric bases Success Metric You can quickly generate appropriate base geometry and transform it systematically for different contexts.🎯 Problem/Goal: Growing 2D shapes into 3D forms and adding surface detail.Window Frame Process Geometry Nodes workflow: Select Faces: Choose wall faces for windows Inset Faces: Create window frame border (0.1m) Extrude Faces: Push inward for depth (-0.05m) Inset Faces (inverse extrude): Inner frame detail (0.02m) Delete Geometry: Remove center faces for opening
Concept Demo Video 📹 gmap395_g_pm_2.2.mp4 A Note of Selections in GN The selection capabilities are somewhat tool specific, it depends greatly on how that particular tool handles geometry data. In Blender GN, selection takes a bit more math or manual work. A hybrid approach of "preprocessing" you geometry and segmenting manually the pieces that need procedural elements is the better approach. With that said, below are some good sources on making selections in GN:
Select What You Want in Geometry Nodes - Blender Tutorial
